strengths: Clean theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 (and its generalization in Appendix A via Savage-Dawid representation) rigorously establishes that a combined correctness + bounded proper scoring rule reward simultaneously incentivizes calibration and correctness, and explains why unbounded scores like log-loss fail this property — a nice, non-trivial piece of decision theory grounding for a practical RL method.

Thorough empirical evaluation across two very different domains (multi-hop QA and math) with multiple out-of-domain generalization datasets (7 total datasets), and a wide set of baselines (BCE classifier, Brier classifier, linear probe, answer-probability), making the comparison reasonably comprehensive.

The finding that RLVR degrades calibration OOD while RLCR improves it, despite comparable in-domain accuracy, is a clear and practically important result with real implications for trustworthy reasoning models.

Interesting and well-motivated downstream analyses: confidence-weighted test-time scaling (best-of-N, majority vote), coherence/self-consistency of confidence across multiple reasoning chains, and probing whether the CoT analysis itself carries calibration-relevant information (Section 4.5) — these extend the paper beyond a single headline metric.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR losing OOD accuracy, residual overconfidence, inter-solution inconsistency), and includes detailed reproducibility information (prompts, training/evaluation setup) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Single base model (Qwen2.5-7B) and single RL algorithm (GRPO variant) are used throughout; no experiments at different scales or with other model families, so it's unclear how well the theoretical guarantees translate into practice as model size/capability changes (the capacity-dependent classifier result in Fig. 5 suggests this could matter significantly).

The RLCR accuracy is sometimes on par with or very slightly below RLVR (e.g., 62.1% vs 63.0% on HotpotQA, 72.7% vs 72.9% on Big-Math) rather than clearly matching it; while differences are small, the paper's framing ('no loss in accuracy') is only loosely supported and lacks statistical significance testing or variance across seeds.

The SFT+RLCR variant shows a fairly large OOD accuracy drop (e.g., 50.9%→43.8% averaged, and dramatic drops on GPQA/CommonsenseQA in Table 7), attributed informally to 'catastrophic forgetting' without deeper investigation — this weakens the practical takeaway of the SFT warmup component, which is otherwise presented as a positive contribution for math calibration.

Reliance on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as an automatic judge for several benchmarks (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA) introduces potential noise/bias into both accuracy and correctness-conditioned calibration metrics, with no human validation or inter-rater agreement reported.

Absolute out-of-domain calibration remains poor even after RLCR (e.g., ECE around 0.21-0.25 in Table 1), and the swarm plot in Fig. 6b shows persistent overconfidence OOD; the paper is upfront about this but it somewhat undercuts the strength of the calibration improvement narrative.

The novelty relative to closely related RL-with-proper-scoring-rule works (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) is incremental — the core technical delta is adding a correctness reward term with a boundedness argument, which, while theoretically clean, is a relatively modest extension over existing calibration-RL literature.

Some experimental design choices are only partially justified, e.g., using different system prompts (Long RLCR vs Simple RLCR) for HotpotQA vs Math based on what 'worked better,' which could reflect prompt-sensitivity in ways not fully characterized.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and increasingly important problem: RLVR-trained reasoning models becoming overconfident/poorly calibrated, especially out-of-distribution.

Provides a clean theoretical result (Theorem 1 and its generalization via the Savage-Dawid representation) showing that combining a bounded proper scoring rule with a correctness reward provably incentivizes both calibration and accuracy, while explaining why unbounded scores like log-loss fail this property — a nice, non-trivial theoretical contribution.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation spanning two training domains (HotpotQA, Big-Math) and seven evaluation datasets, with multiple strong baselines (BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-probability, SFT-warmup variant).

Interesting auxiliary analyses: test-time scaling with verbalized confidence (confidence-weighted majority vote, analysis ensembling), intra-/inter-solution consistency of confidence, and probing whether CoT reasoning is causally useful for calibration via classifier-capacity ablations.
Clear, well-organized writing with illustrative qualitative examples (Appendix D.2) that make failure modes and successes concrete.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base model (Qwen2.5-7B); there is no evidence the approach generalizes across model families or scales, which substantially limits the generality of the claims made in the abstract/conclusion.

No reported variance across seeds/training runs; several accuracy differences between RLCR and RLVR are small (e.g., 62.1% vs 63.0%, 72.7% vs 72.9%) and it is unclear whether these differences (and the calibration gains) are statistically robust rather than single-run artifacts.

The SFT+RLCR variant shows a large OOD accuracy drop (43.8% vs 52.5% for RLVR on math OOD) attributed informally to "catastrophic forgetting" without further diagnosis — this undercuts the paper's central claim that calibration gains come "with no loss in accuracy."

On in-domain evaluation, RLCR's calibration advantage over the much more expensive RLVR+BCE/Brier-classifier baselines is often marginal (e.g., Brier 0.21 vs 0.22 on HotpotQA; ECE actually better for RLVR+classifier than RLCR on some math sub-tables), so the practical benefit over a simple post-hoc classifier is not always convincingly large, especially in-domain where the classifier baseline is already strong.

The causal claim that "reasoning about uncertainty" drives calibration gains (Section 4.5) is weakened by the authors' own finding that at full 7B classifier capacity, the analysis classifier and baseline classifier perform similarly — i.e., the purported benefit of uncertainty CoT content disappears at the scale actually used for the main RLCR model.

Even after RLCR, OOD calibration remains poor in absolute terms (ECE ~0.21–0.25, confidence sums over 1), and the paper's own Fig. 6b shows substantial residual overconfidence OOD, tempering the "substantially improves calibration" framing used in the abstract.

Several evaluation datasets rely on LLM-as-a-judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for correctness, introducing an additional noisy component into both the accuracy and calibration metrics that is not validated or analyzed for judge reliability/calibration bias.

Positioning relative to closest prior work (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025, which already use proper scoring rules as RL rewards for calibration) is somewhat incremental — the core novelty is mainly the addition of the correctness term and application to reasoning-model CoT settings, which, while useful, is a relatively modest technical delta.

No comparison against simple, cheap post-hoc calibration baselines like temperature/Platt scaling on the RLVR model's logits, which would help contextualize how much benefit comes from RL-time optimization versus simple post-processing.

strengths: Provides a clean theoretical justification (Theorem 1 and its generalization to bounded proper scoring rules) for why combining a correctness reward with a Brier-score calibration term yields a reward that is jointly maximized by accurate and calibrated predictions, and clarifies why unbounded scoring rules like log-loss do not have this property.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning both factual QA (HotpotQA, with a thoughtful 'modified' variant that manipulates evidence completeness) and math reasoning (Big-Math/GSM8K/MATH-500), with both in-domain and six/seven out-of-domain transfer datasets.

Strong and diverse baseline suite (RLVR, BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-token-probability), which strengthens the comparison and shows RLCR is competitive with or superior to much more expensive post-hoc calibration methods, especially under distribution shift.

Interesting downstream applications of verbalized confidence beyond calibration metrics: confidence-weighted majority voting / best-of-N for accuracy gains, and ensembling of resampled analyses to further reduce Brier score, demonstrating practical utility of the learned confidence signal.

Additional analyses (classifier-capacity study in Sec 4.5, intra-/inter-solution consistency in Sec 4.6) add depth beyond headline metrics and probe mechanism/robustness questions that many calibration papers skip.
Reasonably transparent reporting of limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR's accuracy drop OOD, residual overconfidence, imperfect inter-solution consistency) rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The claim of 'no loss in accuracy' is not fully supported by the tables: RLCR trained on Big-Math shows a non-trivial OOD accuracy drop relative to RLVR (50.9% vs 52.5%, Table 1b), and SFT+RLCR drops further (43.8%), which is a more substantial trade-off than the abstract/intro suggest.
All experiments use a single base model (Qwen2.5-7B); there is no evidence the approach scales to larger models or transfers across model families, limiting confidence in generality of the findings.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-judge (a relatively small Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for several OOD accuracy evaluations (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA) introduces potential judge noise/bias that is not quantified (e.g., no human-verified subset or inter-judge agreement check).

No seeds/variance reported for the main results, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., small ECE or accuracy gaps between RLCR and classifier baselines) are statistically meaningful.

The two most closely related prior works using proper scoring rules in RL (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) are discussed only qualitatively in related work; no direct empirical comparison against these baselines is provided despite them being the nearest competitors.

Absolute calibration error after RLCR remains fairly high in OOD settings (ECE ~0.21–0.25), and inter-solution confidence sums still noticeably exceed 1 OOD, suggesting the practical reliability gains, while directionally positive, are still limited in absolute terms.

The choice of Brier score versus other bounded proper scoring rules (e.g., clipped log-loss, spherical score) is not empirically ablated, so it is unclear how sensitive results are to this specific design choice despite the generalized theoretical claim.

The format reward used to enforce tag structure is a practical addition not reflected in the core reward equation presented in the theory/method section, which could partially confound the comparison between RLCR and RLVR if it differentially affects training dynamics.

strengths: Clean, well-motivated theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 rigorously shows that combining a bounded proper scoring rule (Brier) with correctness reward jointly incentivizes calibration and accuracy, and the paper carefully explains why unbounded rules like log-loss fail this property (with a nice toy bandit experiment in Appendix E demonstrating the reward-hacking failure mode concretely).

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: results span in-domain and 6-7 out-of-domain datasets across both factual QA (HotpotQA) and math reasoning, with multiple strong baselines (BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-probability, abstention-RL, other calibration-RL variants) and bootstrap confidence intervals.

Strong ablation studies isolating the contribution of explicit uncertainty analysis vs. the calibration-aware reward (Section 4.6, Table 2), providing clear mechanistic insight into what drives the improvements.
Generalization checks across model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3, OLMo-2) in Appendix F strengthen confidence that findings are not specific to one base model.

Useful downstream demonstrations that verbalized confidence improves test-time scaling (confidence-weighted majority vote, best-of-N) and that RLCR improves self-consistency of confidence across reasoning chains, extending the practical relevance beyond calibration metrics alone.

High transparency and reproducibility effort: detailed training/eval setups, prompts, and honest discussion of limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR OOD accuracy drop investigated and partially explained in Appendix J, comparison to closely related concurrent RL-calibration works clearly delineated in Related Work).
weaknesses: Absolute out-of-domain calibration error remains high even for RLCR (e.g., ECE 0.21 on OOD averaged for HotpotQA-trained models), and the paper's own inter-solution consistency analysis (Fig. 4b) shows persistent overconfidence OOD, tempering the practical significance of the gains.

The theoretical result (Theorem 1) is a relatively straightforward application of proper scoring rule theory to a two-term reward; the core novelty is more empirical/engineering (structured CoT + Brier reward) than deeply theoretical, and the framing as a proof-heavy contribution may overstate its technical novelty relative to closely related concurrent work (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025) which the paper itself acknowledges as most closely related.

Accuracy gains from RLCR over RLVR are inconsistent and sometimes RLCR is a few points worse in accuracy (e.g., HotpotQA in-domain 62.1% vs 63.0%), so the 'no cost in accuracy' claim is only approximately true empirically, not always exactly matching the RLVR baseline.

Evaluation relies partly on LLM-as-a-judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for several OOD datasets (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA), which introduces potential noise/bias into both accuracy and calibration metrics that is not deeply analyzed.

The SFT+RLCR variant's OOD accuracy collapse (43.8%) and its partial fix via a one-line prompt tweak (Appendix J) raises concerns about the robustness/reproducibility of reported numbers and suggests results can be sensitive to prompt engineering in ways not fully controlled for across all reported baselines.

Training and evaluation datasets are somewhat narrow in scope (2 RL training domains: HotpotQA-variant and Big-Math), and larger-scale/production-relevant reasoning benchmarks (e.g., competition math, code) are not tested, limiting certainty about broader generalization of the method to more diverse and harder reasoning tasks.

strengths: Clean theoretical contribution (Theorem 1 and its generalization) showing that combining a binary correctness reward with a bounded proper scoring rule (e.g., Brier score) provably incentivizes both calibration and correctness, while explaining why unbounded scores like log-loss can induce reward hacking — this is a nice, rigorous grounding for an otherwise simple reward engineering idea.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two very different domains (multi-hop QA and math), multiple in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, and several strong baselines (BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-probability, abstention-RL, calibration-only RL variants), which gives reasonably convincing evidence that the method outperforms natural alternatives.

Thorough ablation study (Table 2, Appendix G) isolating the contribution of explicit uncertainty reasoning vs. the calibration-aware reward, showing both contribute independently — this adds mechanistic insight beyond just reporting the main result.

Generalization checks across model families (OLMo-2, Qwen3) and the toy bandit experiment comparing Brier vs. log score reward hacking are good-faith efforts to stress-test the theory and demonstrate robustness.

The test-time scaling and self-consistency analyses (confidence-weighted majority vote, intra-/inter-solution coherence) are a nice value-add that ties calibration to a practically useful downstream capability.
weaknesses: The core method is incrementally novel: using proper scoring rules (Brier score) as RL rewards for calibration has already been proposed by Xu et al. (2024) and Stangel et al. (2025); the main novel element here is simply adding a correctness term and extending to reasoning models with verbalized analysis, which is a fairly small conceptual step relative to the amount of machinery (theorems, appendices) built around it.

Accuracy gains from RLCR over RLVR are essentially absent or sometimes negative (e.g., Table 1a: 62.1% vs 63.0% on HotpotQA; Table 1b: similar pattern), and the OOD accuracy improvements are marginal and within noisy ranges across datasets (Appendix L/M show large confidence intervals that often overlap between methods), undermining the claim that RLCR "improves" accuracy rather than merely preserving it.

The SFT+RLCR variant showing a large OOD accuracy drop (52.5%→43.8%) is concerning, and the post-hoc fix (adding one line to the prompt) feels like an ad hoc patch rather than a principled resolution, raising questions about how robust/general the proposed training recipe really is.

Calibration metrics are highly sensitive to the specific OOD dataset (acknowledged by the authors regarding CommonsenseQA), and the overall improvements, while statistically outperforming baselines on average, remain poor in absolute terms (ECE often still 0.2+ OOD), limiting the paper's claimed practical significance.

Evaluation relies substantially on LLM-as-a-judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for several benchmarks (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, CommonsenseQA, GPQA), which introduces an additional noisy, unverified component into both correctness and thus calibration computation, without any validation of judge accuracy/agreement with humans.

The verbalized confidence approach assumes a single scalar probability is sufficient, and the paper's own analysis (Fig. 4b) shows models — including RLCR — still frequently violate basic coherence constraints (confidence sums exceeding 1), suggesting the fundamental approach still only partially addresses the hallucination/overconfidence problem it aims to solve.

Training details (hyperparameters, prompt choices, SFT warmup specifics) are complex and dataset-specific (different prompts and SFT warmup only for Math), raising reproducibility concerns and suggesting that a fair amount of tuning was required to get these results, which is not fully disclosed as a limitation.

strengths: Clean theoretical contribution: a formal proof (Theorem 1, with a more general Corollary using the Savage-Dawid representation) showing that combining a bounded proper scoring rule with a correctness reward simultaneously incentivizes calibration and accuracy, and a clear explanation of why unbounded scores like log-loss break this property.

The toy K-arm bandit experiment nicely corroborates the theory, showing RLCR-Log collapses to degenerate low-confidence abstentions while RLCR-Brier does not, which is a convincing sanity check connecting theory to empirical behavior.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple in-domain and 6+ out-of-domain datasets (QA, multi-hop, factual, math, commonsense, GPQA), with several calibration metrics (ECE, Brier, AUROC) and accuracy, showing RLVR degrades OOD calibration while RLCR consistently improves it.

Strong set of baselines and ablations: post-hoc BCE/Brier classifiers, linear probes, answer-probability baselines, abstention-RL, calibration-only RL variants (full-sequence and partial-sequence), and SFT-warmup variants — this is a thorough comparison against the most relevant prior RL-for-calibration methods (Xu et al., Stangel et al.).
Generalization checks across different base models (OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-8B) and different scoring rules (Brier vs. log score) strengthen the robustness claims.

Useful downstream demonstrations that verbalized confidence can be leveraged for test-time scaling (confidence-weighted majority vote, max-confidence) and coherence analysis (intra-/inter-solution consistency), extending the practical value of calibrated confidence beyond simple ECE reduction.

Honest, self-critical discussion of failure modes and limitations (e.g., SFT+RLCR OOD accuracy drop and root-cause analysis, residual overconfidence in OOD inter-solution consistency, dataset-specific variance such as the CommonsenseQA spurious calibration case).
weaknesses: The core methodological idea—combining a proper scoring rule (Brier) with a correctness reward under RL—is a relatively incremental extension of existing calibration-RL work (Xu et al. 2024; Stangel et al. 2025); the main novelty is the correctness+calibration combination and application to reasoning chains rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Accuracy gains from RLCR over RLVR are often marginal or slightly negative (e.g., Table 1 RLCR slightly underperforms RLVR in-domain on both HotpotQA and Big-Math), and OOD accuracy improvements are generally small, so the main selling point is calibration rather than a joint, strong win on both axes.

Out-of-domain calibration remains poor in absolute terms (ECE ~0.17-0.25) despite being better than baselines, and the paper acknowledges persistent overconfidence and inconsistency across contradictory answers, somewhat limiting the practical significance of the claimed reliability gains.

All main experiments are built around a single base model size (Qwen2.5-7B) for the core results, with other model families relegated to brief appendix checks on a single dataset (HotpotQA); scaling behavior (larger models, where reward hacking is specifically noted as more likely) is not explored despite being flagged as a concern in the related work discussion.

The SFT+RLCR variant shows a substantial generalization/accuracy regression that required post-hoc prompt patching to partially fix, suggesting some fragility in the proposed recipe when combined with warm-start strategies.

Evaluation relies partly on LLM-as-a-judge (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) for several OOD datasets, which introduces an additional source of noise/bias into both accuracy and calibration metrics that is not deeply analyzed.

The theoretical guarantee assumes an idealized setting (expected reward maximization over the true Bernoulli outcome distribution) and does not directly address optimization dynamics under policy-gradient RL with finite samples, limited capacity, or distribution shift, so the practical tightness of the theory-practice connection is somewhat open.
